items.title: Everything that went down at the National Book Awards.
items.summary:
The 77th Annual National Book Awards were announced last night at Cipriani’s Wall Street, a cavernous grey banquet hall that calls Gilded Age villains to mind. I had the good fortune to bear witness to this social event of the season for American letters. What follows is a report from the press table, where I hoovered mac n’ cheese and yearned for opera glasses.

The ceremony kicked off with a performance by Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, who wooed the crowd in a radiant emerald sheath dress. Accompanied by a cellist and keyboard player, Zauner sang her hit “Be Sweet,” and brought some welcome ethereality into the space, which had previously been feeling a little eerie under a dozen red gel lights.

The Red Room motif was a better thematic fit for our host, Special Agent Dale Cooper. But his human avatar Kyle MacLachlan was more inclined to folksy welcome than fever dream. MacLachlan kicked us off with a dramatic reading from the “classic children’s adventure,” Paddle to the Sea . Be sweet, indeed.

After outing himself as a Big Ole Nerd (first favorite books being Dune , The Hobbit ), MacLachlan turned to the publishing landscape and its many concurrent plagues. With the industry facing everything from supply chain issues to ongoing Anthropic lawsuits (first AI mention of many, this night), it was crucial that we gather to celebrate the “irreplaceable power” of storytelling. And so we did.

Author Jason Reynolds presented the Literarian Award for Outstanding Service. He also served the second  look of the night, in a chic textured white tunic. Armed with…

items.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – an intimate meditation on family and memory
items.summary:
The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war

When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.”

Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime.

items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026
items.summary:
This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we . In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them , these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest of us, trying to keep up?

Layli Long Soldier’s We (Wé) takes the question of we to its most elemental level. The Lakota word wé means blood, and Long Soldier uses it to explore family, nation, history, and language through poems, essays, and artwork. For Jake Skeets, we extends beyond people to the land and everything living on it. Horses opens with 200 feral horses stuck in Arizona mud and unfurls into an elegy for a changing Navajo Nation. Fatimah Asghar’s Daughter of the Mountains asks what remains after exile, reckoning with estranged kin and the landscape of their ancestors in poems both funny and elegiac. In Assembled Audience , the ever-delightful Erika Meitner takes up the strange business of being together, on beaches and in airports, in mourning and in protest. William Lessard’s haunting /face turns patents for facial capture technology into unlikely poetry about what happens when a face becomes data. And Hieu Minh Nguyen’s Staying Still traces the distance between the people and places we long to belong to and the selves we’re trying to become.

So much about who counts as us is now decided by people and machines that don’t know us at all. Against all that flattening, these poems get stubbornly specific. Maybe we begins there, not in agreement or allegiance, but in the…

items.title: In the Midst of Bingeing and Purging, My Job Theft Was A Silent Cry for Help
items.summary:
Stealing Space by Dayna Mahannah 

The gas station’s fluorescent lights glowed as I waited for the vehicles to clear their pumps. When the lot had emptied, I abandoned the till. I roamed the aisles, straightening candy products and rearranging the Hungry Man sub sandwiches in the fridge. The security camera had a blind spot where I could wedge myself, right up against the counter. I snuck a Danish, the syrupy glaze clinging to the wrapper like mucus. I chewed fast, facing the wall, and stuffed the packaging in the coffee station trash.

After pretending to organize the chocolate bar display in front of the till, I swiped a Mr. Big off the shelf, tucking it under the edge of my work shirt, and pushed open the side exit into the garage. Light beamed into the defunct repair shop. Dust motes glimmered, floating in the dark like phosphorescent plankton. Then the door shut, severing the shaft of light. Petroleum wafted up from the concrete floor. Standing on the stoop, my skin hot despite the frigid shop, I tore through the serrated edge of the candy wrapper, scarfing the chewy mess. I jammed the yellow wrapper underneath used oil containers in the recycling drum.

We experimented with tiny crimes like egging houses and stealing makeup from Zellers.

Back inside the station, a cursory check out the window showed no customers gassing up. I flipped the Back in 5 Minutes sign on the front door, turned the lock, raced for the bathroom, and drove my fingers down my esophagus until everything pushed out into the open.

I’d started working at the gas station in June, just as grade 10…

items.title: Best Romance Books of the Year
items.summary:
As 2026 comes to a close and we officially enter cuffing season, it’s time for us to look back at the romance books that had our hearts pounding. Winter months are the perfect time to cuddle up with a love story (or five), so here are the best romance books of the year. Were all of these on your radar? Is there a must-read romance you have yet to discover? Read on to find out!

Die for Me by Shirlene Obuobi 
 What makes Shirlene Obuobi’s latest novel stand out as one of the best of the year is the way it expertly blends multiple genres in a fun and engaging way. Paranormal romance, psychological thriller, medical drama, gothic horror, urban fantasy… this story has it all. Sean is a 38 year-old interventional cardiologist who isn’t looking for love, but then she meets Julian. Julian is devastatingly charming, mysterious, and eleven years Sean’s junior. And by the time Sean falls hard for him, she realizes Julian is much more dangerous than he first appears. 

The Bad Boyfriend Curse by Farah Heron 
 Fans of contemporary YA rom coms and fake dating stories need to pick up The Bad Boyfriend Curse, the absolute best YA romance of the year. Raised by a single mom, Meera has always believed that the women in her family are cursed to date men who will ultimately destroy their lives. To evade the curse, Meera spends her whole life playing it safe. Yet somehow Meera’s first date ends with an arrest and community service. Since being the “good girl” has gotten her nowhere, Meera decides she will “date” another bad boy to get back at her mom. But what happens when the bad boy she…
items.t: Best Romance Books of the Year

items.title: Best Sci-Fi and Fantasy Books of the Year
items.summary:
This year will go down as one in which we needed to escape to worlds of make-believe more than ever, and thankfully, science fiction and fantasy authors answered the call! This year was full of incredible novels, more than we could possibly list here, but these five are stellar examples of how rewarding it has been to be an SFF reader in 2026.

Be sure to check out Book Riot’s full Best Books of 2026 list , which includes more awesome sci-fi and fantasy picks!

2 of My Favorite Science Fiction & Fantasy Books of 2026 

The Girl with a Thousand Faces by Sunyi Dean 
 If you like your fantasy on the darker side, this criminally overlooked work of historical fiction is for you! It’s a gorgeous and scary novel about a woman who lives in Kowloon Walled City. Mercy arrived in Hong Kong decades before with no memory of her past, and has made her living working for the local crime syndicate as a ghost talker. But when a particularly nasty spirit starts drowning people, it turns out it has ties to Mercy. And maybe if she can remember where she came from, she can stop it.

Earth 7 by Deb Olin Unferth 
 This is a delicious work of literary sci-fi with such amazing writing and imagination, it almost feels like it could be real. In the future, Earth is a burned-up wasteland, and people have to find other places to live. Some reside in pods in the ocean, while others move to Mars. One woman, who was raised in an ocean pod by her cold and distant scientist mother, becomes fascinated by sand. items.title: 6 of the Best Children’s Books of the Year
items.summary:
Most folks in the children’s book industry will agree that 2026 has been a bit of a rough year in publishing. Picture book publishers have tightened up their lists, focusing on titles they know will sell well, like humor and books by celebrity authors. Middle grade has struggled for longer , but it’s nice to see publishers figuring out what kids want to read, like slimmer, more graphic-heavy books that still have plenty for readers to dig into. 

Though it always feels a bit impossible to pick and choose, as 2026 comes to a close, we’ve rounded up our favorite children’s books of the year, from imaginative picture books in translation to compelling middle grade full of friend drama.

Watermelon Pool by Bonsoir Lune, translated by Frances Cha 
 If ever there was a book that made you want to climb inside its pages and immerse yourself in the full sensory experience, it’s this one. It’s a regular tradition in the village to split open a giant watermelon and enjoy a refreshing swim each summer. Children laugh alongside adults, all of whom enjoy using the various parts of the watermelon for diving, jumping, and otherwise lounging in the pool. When summer comes to an end, the pool closes up shop, and the villagers eagerly await the next year. This joy-filled, colorful picture book is one where you’ll be able to hear every single page. —Kelly Jensen

items.title: Must-Visit Indie Bookstores with Cozy and Whimsical Vibes
items.summary:
Rebecca McKee is the author of Mr. Mendlebee’s Pandimensional Literary Repository (and Yarn) , out this week from G. P. Putnam’s Sons. Below, she recommends six indie bookstores that inspired the novel. 

After living in seven different states, I know two things to be absolutely true: 1) there is magic everywhere, and 2) that magic is usually housed in your local indie bookstore. When I wrote Mr. Mendlebee’s Pandimensional Literary Repository (and Yarn) , I wanted the repository to be as magical as the real-life bookstores I had visited across the U.S. Here is a list of just a few of the incredible shops that inspired Mr. Mendlebee’s.

Boarding House Books | Claremore, OK 

A sweet little shop nestled among antique stores on historic Will Rogers Boulevard. If you’ve never encountered a clawfoot bathtub full of romance paperbacks, you’ll want to make a trip here.

Federal Street Books | Greenfield, MA 

Woman-owned, community-focused, and packed to the gills with great titles. When you see the stairs to the basement, you’ll think, This does not seem like a basement I should be in, right? Go to the basement. You’ll thank me later.

Gardner’s Used Books & Music | Tulsa, OK 

An incredible 23,000-square-foot labyrinth of just about any kind of media you can imagine: books, comics, games, a disconcerting cardboard cutout of James Patterson. Wander deep enough and you’ll find yourself at the taped outline of a book lover who never found their way out.

The Haunted Bookshop | Iowa City, IA 

Cats, narrow alcoves packed with treasures, and a lovingly-curated collection of both…

items.title: The More, the Merrier: Michelle Tea On the Possibilities of Polyamory
items.summary:
My first marriage was illegal. Well, we weren’t breaking any laws, I guess, so it wasn’t illegal , just not legal. I eloped with my trans boyfriend, Aldo, following a regular Bingo party at my house. The Bingo party at least was illegal. In the long list of illicit activities that occurred in the Blue House, the queer, punk household where I spent my twenties, a little Bingo game among friends who drank beer and ashed their cigarettes on my floor might seem like small potatoes, but we were playing for cash, so it was technically an illicit gambling ring. One night, after the game disbanded, me and Aldo absconded to the home of Jo-Jo and Tommy, an elder butch-femme couple, low-key famous for having made award-winning lesbian porn movies, and throwing sex parties in the loft where their open marriage thrived.

Jo-Jo was a witch, and when I’d asked her to marry Aldo and me, she took it very seriously. Her fee was $19.99, some of which she spent on a sheet cake from Safeway. Aldo, while browsing the veritable bazaar that lined the streets near my home—blankets covered with all sorts of goods being sold by unhoused neighborhood denizens—spotted a silky, shiny, pale blue dress and asked if he could buy it. Only if you promise me a pretty girl’s gonna get married in it , the proprietor said, and just like that my wedding dress was blessed by the streets. For a veil I popped by a Target, and in the children’s department found a crown woven with ribbon the same pearly blue as my dress, stuck with fake butterflies. I was ready for my elopement.

items.title: The Years When Gospel Artists Went Platinum
items.summary:
Perhaps the first time I realized the power and impact of gospel music, I was no more than six years old. I woke up in the middle of the night for some reason. All was dark and quiet except for the music coming from the clock radio that my mother kept on the kitchen counter. When I was little, the carpet covering the threshold of my bedroom door used to scare me so badly that I would not want to leave my room at night. When the bedroom was dark and the hallway’s light hit the threshold, the otherwise beige carpet would look like a dark and stormy sea of Texas-sized bugs to my young eyes—impenetrable. But, that night, it was too dark for me to see imagined critters, and the music was too beautiful. That night, I left my bedroom and walked down the hallway until I was inches from the radio. As the perennial 12:00 midnight flashed red (as the time on the clock needed to be set), Andraé Crouch and his singing compatriots belted:

We need to hear from you

We need a word from you

If we don’t hear from you

What will we do?

And, in that cozy two-bedroom apartment on the southwest side of Houston, Texas, while my family slept, I stood captivated as the gospel sounds washed over me. This memory of hearing that song play on the kitchen clock radio remains a poignant one for me. It marks the beginning of my enduring relationship with gospel music.

items.title: If I See an Author Out to Lunch, Am I the Asshole for Approaching Them?
items.summary:
Hey there, howdy!

Welcome back to the most marvelously drunken advice column on the planet. That’s right, it’s time for another stellar installment of Am I the Literary Asshole, a place where movers and shakers come to both move and shake. I’m your host, Kristen Arnett, and it’s time for us to get down to business. That’s right, we’ve got a truckload of exciting quandaries awaiting us today, so I’d like to jump straight into things with some pomp and much circumstance.

Let’s get some icy cold martinis going and sip at them while we take a gander at our first question, shall we?

1)  Is it in bad taste to approach authors in their “off” time? Say, perhaps, when they’re out to lunch or dinner and away from the hubbub of something like AWP or at a festival or after a reading? Thank you for your time! 

I think we’ve answered a version of this question before, but I don’t think there’s anything wrong we’ve approaching it again for new readers to the column. And since I just got done hanging out at Texas Book Festival last weekend, I feel especially ready to chat.

This is going to play out much like it would in any other regular social situation. Before approaching the author in question, you must first read the room.

Is the person with their children? Are they on the phone? Are they carrying lots of bags, lugging around a giant suitcase, or are they in the middle of paying the check and/or talking to a waiter? Are they ordering coffee? Are they typing very furiously on their computer or speaking in whispers, privately, to another person? Are they kissing their partner or…

items.title: How Bookselling Saved My Writing Life
items.summary:
From 2017 to 2022 I was working on a book I loved, a quiet novel about three girls growing up in Wisconsin. The manuscript seemed promising at first. Its first chapter won me a fellowship back to the University of Wisconsin, where I had completed my MFA a year earlier, and whose generous faculty and staff supported me as I drafted my first novel. But when my agent and I submitted my second book to publishers in 2022, we didn’t get the response we were hoping for. Rather than continue to submit to a second round of editors, my agent suggested that I start another novel, something bigger and plottier and splashier, something more well-suited to the market we were in, a market that was becoming increasingly difficult for literary fiction.

I had spent five years on the novel, and my agent’s advice plunged me into a deep depression. On top of my sadness were layers of bitterness and spite. My largely unexamined assumptions about genre and where literary fiction fit in made “commercial” writing seem necessarily inauthentic. Still raw from rejection, I questioned what I was even doing. What was the point of writing fiction—especially literary fiction—in the first place?

I received each gift with the sincerity in which it was offered, and it was this generosity that reminded me of why I write in the first place. To connect with readers.

Literary fiction asks so much of a reader. Without genres and tropes to fall back on, a literary reader must be up for anything. To pick up a novel is to catapult yourself into the lives of others and exercise empathy without the guarantee of…
items.t: How Bookselling Saved My Writing Life

items.title: You Don Chop? On Food as Love in Nigerian Culture
items.summary:
Different cultures have different ways of saying, “I care about you.” In Nigeria, we start by asking about your well-being (How you dey? How’s the family? How’s work? How are your parents? And even how’s school? You answer each one with fine).

Then comes the question that actually matters: you don chop? Which means, have you eaten?

Growing up, I saw this everywhere, and it reminded me that food, more than anything else, is how we take care of one another.

The answer “I’m fine” won’t satisfy anyone. It’s either a yes or no. Either admit you haven’t eaten or give a full account of what you ate, where you ate it, and who cooked it. Nobody is checking on your stomach; rather, they’re asking if you’re well taken care of.

Feed the body first, sort every wahala later. Nigerians believe you can’t face your problems on an empty stomach.

Growing up, I saw this everywhere, and it reminded me that food, more than anything else, is how we take care of one another. Whenever you go to Nigerian events—weddings, funerals, child naming ceremonies, birthday parties—one thing is constant, and it’s always served first. Puff Puff. You take one or two (not more) unless you want to attract side-eyes.

If you’ve never had it, it’s soft dough made with flour, water, yeast, sugar, and anything else you’d like to add, deep-fried in hot oil. They’re soft on the outside but fluffy and slightly chewy inside. It’s sweet without being too sweet, and it will have you saying, “ Can I have some more, please?” 

(Pro tip: Best eaten while hot.)

Before the jollof rice, soup and eba, or pepper soup, there…

But Promise Me, America treats all such inquiries as extraneous and gratuitous…Biden allows that his June, 2024, debate with Donald Trump (who had his own issues with classified documents) had ‘gone badly’ but adds that ‘debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent Presidents.’ He sees no qualitative distinction between his frightening and heartbreaking lack of focus that night and Barack Obama’s subpar performance against Mitt Romney, or George W. Bush being ‘caught with a scowling face’ in his debate with John Kerry.

Apart from the few, frustrating stretches on his reëlection decision (from which one would never know that he had once referred to himself as ‘a bridge,’ a phrase widely understood to mean that he would serve only a single term), most of Promise Me, America is startlingly dull. Much of it has the feel of…

items.title: We Belong to the Trees
items.summary:
Pa was a farmer. He was also a hunter. When people came to their farmhouse in Tzaneen, they were welcomed by a bush-buck’s head nailed to the living-room wall. Its eyes bugged out, staring into nothing.

Pa was proud of it. He always showed it off to his friends with a wide smile across his face, while playing with his long beard. His teeth flashed when he told them how he’d shot the buck with the first bullet from his tall hunting rifle. That was how Nicolas knew his father was proud—because Pa rarely revealed his teeth. He never smiled at him or Ma. Only when he talked about hunting did Nicolas see that his teeth existed, and that they were yellow as dark pee.

Nicolas was there when Pa shot the buck, two years earlier. That was the last, and only, time Pa took him hunting. Nicolas had cried that entire afternoon because he’d heard the buck wail for its Ma and Pa as it fell to the ground.

In the bakkie, with the dead bushbuck lying in the back, Pa had scolded him: “Jy is ’n Boer, you will always be a Boer—hunting is in your blood. So stop crying like a little girl. Hoor jy my?”

Nicolas had nodded, sobbing into his trembling hands. “I said stop crying, Nico!” he’d shouted.

There was also a young kudu’s horns and a rhino horn on Pa’s bedroom wall. But he never showed them to anyone. When the farmworkers caused trouble and the police came by, Pa hid the horns.

One time, the workers stole his oranges. Another time, they protested for a month and said they wanted a pay increase. Pa covered the horns with a sheet before the police arrived. After they left, he’d complained…
items.t: We Belong to the Trees

items.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
items.summary:
This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention

American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch.

Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.

Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.

Revered historian, author and francophile with a novelistic approach to his subject

On the website the Oxford Muse, which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.”

During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. That is also what conversation seeks.”

items.title: Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era
items.summary:
The Original Mother 

The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy . “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the door a short while ago. 

“A man.”

“Huh.”

“Selling fish from a pole,” the original mother said.

Her husband dug at his jaw. “Who is Vasco . . .” he said. “Vasco da Gama!”

“Is that his name?”

Her husband’s face fell. “Huh?”

“The man,” the original mother said, suddenly finding herself curious for anything that might shed light on the stranger that had come to their door. “Does he sell fish here often? Vasco?”

“Oh, right,” her husband said, concentrating on the next clue. “Sure.” He wriggled his toes. His ankle let out a frivolous little crack.

They lapsed into silence. 

The original mother pursed her lips and tried to clip his gray toenails, but the hot ache in her old, arthritic fingers was too much to bear. 

“Ah . . . oh! What is the Law of Reflection?” her husband said. 

The original mother let her eyes go soft. Her husband’s toes grew indistinct. As she reckoned with the crude geometry of this latest defeat, another woman, her mirror image, brought out a second pair of toenail clippers, sat cross-legged before the La-Z-Boy, and steadied the husband’s other foot with her right hand. 

The original mother’s husband jerked the legrest down and grasped both women by their wrists, shaking the toenail clippers from their hands. The mothers appraised each…

items.title: Two Trans Novelists Have Broken the National Book Awards’ Glass Ceiling
items.summary:
Tonight the winners of the 77th National Book Awards will be announced. Though this will be published before we know which authors ultimately receive the grand honor, I already know that the finalists this year uniquely—and with exquisite, hard-earned artistic merit—speak to the ever-evolving state of American literature.

Two of the finalists for the National Book Award in Fiction are trans—only the second and third openly trans authors ever to be nominated in this category. At no fault of trans writers, and all fault of the societal powers that be: This simply was not possible even a decade ago. If we’re not careful, it might not be possible once again, even before the next presidential term. It’s for this reason, additional to the fact of their literary genius, that I consider myself greatly privileged to spotlight National Book Award finalists Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera.

From untangling the increasingly hostile and anti-trans US political landscape in Thomas’s Mad Eden , to exploring Colombia’s lively queer underground scene in Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You , both of these authors’ novels prove to be unprecedented in craft, and unchallengeably excellent. Over Zoom, email, and voice notes, Thomas, Lopera, and I discussed the complexity of labels in trans and neurodivergent communities, the nuances of capturing queer joy, and the difficult onus of representation for minority authors.

Jalen Giovanni Jones: So first, I’d like to congratulate you both on the many accolades that these beautiful novels brought you, particularly you both being…

items.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
items.summary:
Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war

Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style.

Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “gjak” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

Continue reading...
items.t: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle

items.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
items.summary:
Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion

Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

items.title: Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible
items.summary:
Rumor has it that now—in our world of alternative facts, of journalists replaced by influencers, experts replaced by AI, and of news constantly deemed fake—we’ve finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “truth.” Hard data is tough to come by, since sensationalism’s better for algorithms. It’s difficult to tell if any given video is secretly an ad. Not even our Google searches can be trusted. They’re calling it a “post-truth society,” and here we are, left in constant skepticism over the fabric of our reality. Did we really have a White House Press Secretary between October 12th and October 16th, 2026? Is Manon of KATSEYE really on “hiatus”? Could we really “see everything”? Ugh. We can’t even trust our documentaries anymore.

Multi-award-winning, National Book Award longlisted author Nafissa Thompson-Spires knows none of this is new. Her second book and debut novel, The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford (a current First Novel Prize finalist) is set in the all-Black town of 1920s Newville, where the town has finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “Richard Milford.” An infamous moonshiner, an unloyal womanizer, and just plain mean, the town will tell you—collectively—that this is good riddance. That is, except for his four wives and his beloved housekeeper Alberta. They’d surely remember him differently, right? Unless they somehow had reason to kill him . . . Wait, how many times did Rich die?

With slick wit, a wry sense of dark humor, and a hefty dose of whimsy, Thompson-Spires deconstructs the idea of truth before our…
items.t: Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible

items.title: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence
items.summary:
The Italian who became kingmaker in the world’s largest democracy charts her remarkable journey

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.

No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.

Continue reading...

items.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
items.summary:
Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood

Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place.

Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its…

items.title: I Want to Have a Baby Because I Miss the Violence
items.summary:
An excerpt from Nanny Nanny by K Chiucarello 

I had a feeling this was coming when Michael began texting heavily a few days ago. On the first snow of the season, he texted to say he’d had a dream about Jenny.

You know your friend Jenny? he asked me.

Jenny, as in my best friend? I replied.

Exactly, he said.

In the dream Jenny had gotten a tattoo of a tampon on the back of her leg, right in the ditch behind the knee, which I hear is one of the most painful body parts to place something permanent. Michael thought it was funny and specific that Jenny had appeared to him in the night and that a tampon was involved.

He texted, Do you remember telling me about those, about periods and the smell of rust that hits the nose when a flood opens like that?

In high school, I had been the first to teach him all about tampons. We were in his Buick when I explained to him all the chores women must suffer through when they begin their periods. There’s ruined jeans, I told him, and heating pads, long hours of lying horizontal or moving through the world with cotton shoved into you. A string. A metallic smell, I said, crinkling my poreless face. Here, I said, leaning over to Michael from the passenger seat. Smell this. And I shoved a fake gold bracelet my mother had purchased for me into his nose.

It’s certainly a smell, he replied, reclining back into the driver’s seat.

So. Michael had this dream about Jenny getting a tampon tattoo and he texted me, coming back into my life like clockwork, like he does every season.

We never could stop speaking for good, despite both of us acting,…

items.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.summary:
Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough

In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

items.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
items.summary:
From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy

In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.
